articles.description:
extolling the power of plain text. It’s a notion that’s familiar to all us Emacs users and even more so to Org users. We Org users (or more generally Markdown and other markup users) can write plain text and have it formatted for output in a variety of ways. The point is, the text stays text and is readable even without the formatting.


As nickb says, text written today will still be readable 50 years from now. Sure, UTF-8 and the other Unicode formats can and do add new characters from time to time but text written today will have the same meaning even if new characters are added.


The most important aspect is that you’ll own your data no matter what programs come and go. Emacs isn’t going anywhere but even if it did, it wouldn’t matter. Text will still be readable and something like Org or Markdown will still make intended formatting obvious even if Org and Markdown no longer exist.


Nickb acknowledges that text is not the right answer for everything. You wouldn’t, for example, want to represent a photograph in plain text and there are lots of other examples. Still, for many applications, plain text is not only sufficient but probably the better solution.

articles.description:
David Pape asked:




I just typed



>Closes: #47, #48, #49, #50, #51, #52, #53, #54



into a commit description, all by hand.



Is there a way in Emacs to expand some kind of range description to make this easier? 😅



I want to expand strings like "5-10, 15-18, 3" into numbers.




Hmm, could be useful. It reminds me of how page ranges work, which will be handy if I want to tinker with PDFs. Let's see if something like this works:




(defun sacha-parse-page-range (s)
  "Parse a page range string and return a list of numbers.
Ex: 1-5
2-4, 6-10
1 4 7-9
3-11/2   - this one specifies an increment"
  (seq-mapcat
   (lambda (part)
     (let ((nums (mapcar 'string-to-number (split-string part " *[-/] *"))))
       (if (= (length nums) 1)
           nums
         (number-sequence (elt nums 0) (elt nums 1) (elt nums 2)))))
   (split-string s "[, \t\n\r]+")))

(ert-deftest sacha-parse-page-range ()
  (should (equal (sacha-parse-page-range "5-10")
                 '(5 6 7 8 9 10)))
  (should (equal (sacha-parse-page-range "1-5, 8")
                 '(1 2 3 4 5 8)))
  (should (equal (sacha-parse-page-range "1 4 7-9")
                 '(1 4 7 8 9)))
  (should (equal (sacha-parse-page-range "3-11/2")
                 '(3 5 7 9 11))))

(defun sacha-issue-range (range)
  "Expand RANGE to a list of issues and insert them."
  (interactive "MRange (ex: 1-5, 7): ")
  (let ((s (mapconcat (lambda (n) (format "#%d" n))
                      (sacha-parse-page-range range)
                      ", ")))
    (when (called-interactively-p 'any)
      (insert s))
    s))

This is part of my EmacsConfiguration.

So it is with the Triode app for macOS, which leverages Cocoa frameworks (App Intents in particular) to support remote control.
triode.el is an Emacs Lisp library which provides a simple remote control interface to the Triode app. Basic support for selecting a radio station, play/stop, and muting are provided. Not every feature in the Triode app is accessible to triode.el though; this is controlled by the App Intents actually implemented by its developer, The Iconfactory.

shazam.el - Interface for Shazam music recognition.
All the above efforts have been an exploration of malleable computing using Emacs as the main orchestration tool. I plan on posting a more technical deep dive reflecting this work in the not too distant future. That said, if you’re a macOS user who uses Emacs and Triode, I encourage you to give triode.el a try. articles.description:
What’s the future of Emacs? He asks that question in the context of assuming that Emacs will continue to exist for any timeline that matters to us. But how, he asks, will we use it?


The answer that will occur to most of us is speech mediated input á la Star Trek TNG. We’ll simply tell Emacs what we want it to do and it will do it. But think about that for a moment. Would you really want to dictate the code for your latest program to the computer? Or would you even want to dictate your documentation, story, or letter to your computer?


Sure, you could say something like, “Computer write a program to do such and such.” but then you’re not using Emacs at all. The same for asking the computer to write something for you. That—more or less—is here today but most of us don’t like the results and, again, we’re not really using Emacs in those situations.


For my part, my written thoughts are always much better organized than my spoken ones so even with  capable voice input, I’d much prefer to use the keyboard. Maiorana agrees. He points back to a couple of episodes from Tales From the Darkside1 in which people use the keyboard to do magic with the computer. For him, Meta+x is the spell that enables the magic and he’s very attached to it. Like me, he doesn’t anticipate abandoning the keyboard.


What do you think? Will we still use the keyboard or will we move on to something better?

Earlier this year I added Ghostel to my
Emacs configuration. Ghostel is a terminal emulator for Emacs that uses
Ghostty's engine underneath. It is a delight to use
especially with the TUI applications.
Nested Emacs frame problem
I use Emacs in daemon
mode,
and then use emacsclient to open new frames from the daemon. To use the same
Emacs daemon when opening files through other programs such as git, sops, I have
a small shell script ee configured as my default EDITOR. It opens a new
Emacs frame in the terminal.
#!/bin/sh

exec emacsclient --create-frame --no-window-system "$@"

When I run this script from Ghostel, it opens a nested Emacs frame in Ghostel's
terminal session.

Solution
Emacs sets an environment variable INSIDE_EMACS for shells and subprocesses.
The script use this variable to check if it is launched from Ghostel and use the
--reuse-frame flag to open the new buffer in the current frame.
#!/bin/sh

if [ "$INSIDE_EMACS" = "ghostel" ]
then
  exec emacsclient --reuse-frame "$@"
fi

exec emacsclient --create-frame --no-window-system "$@"

What is spook?
  The Emacs function spook is
  not what you think it is.  It doesn't make creepy noises, draw scary
  ASCII art or change the theme to orange on black.  In fact it has
  nothing at all to do with Halloween, ghosts, monsters, pandemics or
  IRS audits.



What it does is insert words and phrases into the current buffer "to
help give your message ... attractiveness for automated keyword
scanners."



What kind of words or phrases might you expect to see?  To find out I
invoked spook while composing this content.  Here's what
it added:




    TELINT Drug North Korea Security Consulting Virii Abu Ghraib Fort
    Hancock CUD AMEMB Vaccine MARTA racal E.O.D. Blizzard Nigeria
  



  It's easy1 to configure spook to insert an alternate set
  of words and phrases -- just change the file name in the
  variable spook-phrases-file from "spook.lines" to the
  name of the alternate file.  Unfortunately it must reside in the
  Emacs data directory; the file's location is fixed.  The variable
  can be found in the Spook customization group, whose parent group is
  Games.



  Even with only 72 lines in its source code file,2 spook
demonstrates how to insert one or more random lines from a file into
the current buffer.



  1 It's "easy" if you have Administrator permissions.



  2 The 72 lines is the entire spook.el file; the first 48%
of the file provides the usual comments that describe the GNU GPL,
author, maintainer info as well as documentation.

keybinding (C-c C-x C-t) --

in the middle.



When I pressed that key combination (inadvertently), all the
YYYY-MM-DD timestamps in the buffer were converted to the MM/DD/YYYY
format.  This was unacceptable -- I needed to change them back.
However undo did not revert the timestamps; it just undid
the last edit.  Furthermore, these undesired timestamps couldn't be
edited and were impervious to org-shiftright.  I was
confused yet again.



I didn't even know how this happened.  So I
invoked view-lossage as a kind reader once suggested 1
and discovered org-toggle-timestamp-overlays.



The docstring was no help – it's self-evident that it would "Toggle
the use of custom time stamp formats."  Eager to clock out of my task,

I figured that since it toggles the timestamp, all I had to do was
invoke it again to toggle it back.  Nope.  Well, a nice message
appears, saying "Time stamp overlays removed."  Yet the timestamps
looked the same.



Undaunted, I figured I'd reload the buffer with org-mode-restart.
That had no effect.  To finally fix this, I deleted the buffer and
revisited the file.



A command like this surely is in the same category as upcase-region,
which is disabled by default.  And so this is why I added

Aquí, is sort of a niche application but is potentially useful for more than just its intended use.


The back story is that Choi really likes the sunrise-sunset command in Emacs that tells him the times that the sun rises and sets. The problem is that sunrise-sunset requires that you first specify the latitude and longitude of where you want to know the times. The standard way of doing that is to record them in your init.el, which is what I do. Choi, however, travels with his laptop but still wants to know when the sun is coming up or going down. There’s no automatic way of setting the information so he wrote Aquí to provide it. The only downside is that it works exclusively on the Mac platform.


Once installed, all you need do is call aqui to set all the appropriate information. I hardly ever travel these days so I wasn’t going to bother but it’s easy to use and can give you your current latitude and longitude as well as your address so I thought, “Why not?”. After I installed and ran it, it gave me my exact address as well as my latitude and longitude. That might sometimes vary a bit depending on the vagaries of GPS but it’s certain to be close.


If you decide to try it out, be sure to take a look at the user manual so see what commands are available. Mostly, though, you’ll just need to run aqui. Also be sure to check out the installation section because you need to install a shortcut. That’s just a matter of clicking on a link in the manual but Aquí won’t work until you do.

in-memory cache for Denote. It can be used to speed up certain
computationally expensive operations. It must be opt-in because there
are many users, myself included, who do not need such functionality (I
program because the challenge is fun, just how I did with denote-sequence, for example).
I have a final update on this that I posted on denote.git issue 724 
and am copying below. Any future changes will appear in the release
notes of the next version of Denote. In short: it is happening.
The status update on denote.git
Hello again folks!
I have an update on the denote-data project. The code is in this denote.git branch for now: https://github.com/protesilaos/denote/tree/denote-data
What I am doing:
Find the computationaly heavy functions.
Write denote-data variants for them.
Introduce variables to funcall VAR instead of calling the heavy functions directly.
Make the denote-data-mode set those variables.
This way we can have any extension do what denote-data does. And this way denote-data can be its own package as well.
The first big problem I see now is how to make the caching functions async. I will figure this out by studying list-packages and related.
Then I want to study filenotify.el. @mentalisttraceur I have noted that your code is okay for copyright purposes, so I can check it out. Or you can send a PR, if you prefer.
Otherwise, I think this is almost done.
With an opt-in cache we can support other workflows that people have been asking for, such as in-buffer completion.

One of my favorite Emacs commands is sunrise-sunset (Sunrise/Sunset (GNU Emacs Manual)) to get the day’s times for sunrise and sunset. For it to work right, you must have Emacs pre-configured with location information. This is done by setting three customizable variables:

If you run Emacs on a system that is fixed in location, manually setting the above variables is a one time task. However if you do a fair amount of traveling with Emacs on a laptop, a more programmatic solution might be desired using a location service, ideally an OS-native one. If you’re a macOS user, Aquí (aqui.el) does just that by invoking a Shortcut to query the OS-native location service.
Leveraging Shortcuts gives Emacs access to a high-accuracy fused location update without need to build, install, and configure a separate macOS executable.

1

wrote back in July, although I’ve had Embark installed for some time, I’ve only just begun to really use it. Most of my uses involve following a link (of any type) and acting on a group of files, typically to delete several files at once. Of course, those uses are barely scratching the surface of Embark’s capabilities.


Those capabilities are essentially open ended. By that I mean you can define your own Embark actions. Stefano Rodighiero has a nice example of this. It’s a nice example for two reasons. First, it’s simple and easy to follow even though—the second reason—I don’t know anything about what he’s trying to do.  The point is that Rodighiero has an obscure—to me—application that he wants to provide an action for but you don’t need to know the details of the application to follow the action.


This is incredibly powerful. Rodighiero let Embark do the hard work of identifying and parsing the target and merely wrote some simple glue to take that target reference and do something useful with it.


If, like me, you’re just beginning to feel your way around Embark, Rodighiero’s post is a useful read. You almost certainly won’t have a need to copy his action but it’s an excellent go by for your own.

You've been fighting it off as best you can, but the weight of the evidence is starting to hit your hips, knees and ankles in a series of small electric spasms. You've tried to explain it away as "Well, the league's weird this year," and while you're right no matter what league you're referring to, the disorientation is still there and getting worse.
The Tampa Bay Rays look like they are going to win their American League Division Series, but that's not the thing that's making you nickname your persistent migraine as though it were a mischievous nephew. It's that they're making the New York Yankees look like the Los Angeles Angels, which is not just laughing at the power of branding but making a fresh mockery of a town that already has to put up with the Mets.
The Rays gnaw at a game like hyperactive beavers, eschewing home runs (except for Junior Caminero) and embracing the annoying little things that modern baseball once disdained: speed, defense, and even the occasional bunt. The Yankees have struggled with stuff like catching the ball or throwing it in a useful direction, which have always been in fashion. That is how Game 2, a 5-2 Rays win, played out Monday night. The Yankees' four errors were spectacular, the second-most put up by the team in its 448 all-time postseason games, highlighted but by no means concluded by Jazz Chisholm Jr.'s comprehensive mangling of a double-play pivot on the Rays' third at-bat of the game. Had it not been for Ben Rice's two solo homers, the Yankees would have looked utterly Angelic in all the worst ways.

The first thing I have to warn you is that if you purchase Josh Malerman's Incidents Around The House, it will have a sticker on it saying it's a movie now. If that's a dealbreaker, there's no escaping it, because the movie is coming out next week and because it features one of the all-time fucked-up jump scares in a trailer. I almost can't believe that was allowed. Anyway, yes, this is the book that Other Mommy is based on. But several Defector staffers have previously read it and won't shut up about how good it is.
The second thing to warn you about is that this book is scary. I am not a baby, and I read a decent amount of horror, and it's been a long, long time since I read anything that had me jumpy about leaving my bed in the middle of the night. My all-time favorites are Shirley Jackson's The Haunting of Hill House and Michael McDowell's The Elementals, and I won't really hesitate to put Incidents up there with those. It's not postmodern/lit/"elevated horror," like so many of today's horror novelists seem to aspire to. This is the classic shit.
Incidents Around The House is narrated by Bela, an 8-year-old girl who for some time has been visited by ... something that lives in her closet, but is not confined to it. She calls this something Other Mommy, because it looks like her mother—mostly, and sometimes—and it asks her, in increasingly threatening tones, if it can go inside her heart. She tells her parents about Other Mommy, and the book is about them not trying to figure out what it is, but rather if there is any way to escape it.

The Arizona State hockey team plays their home opener on Friday, but hanging over their season, and the entire program, will be what happened to defenseman Matthew Mayich. At an outdoor, "military-style" team workout on Aug. 20, Mayich collapsed from exertional heat stroke. He's been in the hospital on life support ever since, with his family attorneys saying that he has "zero chance" of making a complete recovery.
Mayich's hospitalization has shone a harsh light on both the ASU administration and the wider culture of "military-style" workouts in athletics. The guy who ran this ASU workout, Tim Ziesel, is a former Army Green Beret who pushed the players through intense exercises in high-80s heat with limited water, and he ordered extra running for those who didn't perform to his specifications. An Ontario native and 2023 St. Louis Blues draft pick who transferred to ASU from Clarkson University in upstate New York, Mayich was one of 18 new players on the roster this season and was unused to the Arizona climate, putting him more at risk for heat stroke. According to The Athletic, when Mayich collapsed to the ground, "he stayed in the sun for several minutes before four players carried him into the shade."
The workout was symbolic of a philosophy that head coach Greg Powers, the only man to coach the program since it joined D-I in 2015, attempted to implement after a lackluster end to the previous season. “I hate to say the word ‘soft,’ but that’s what we were,” Powers said in May. “And it became contagious." Per The Athletic, he was known around the program for a quick temper and a willingness to insult his players. Ziesel's whole deal seems specifically engineered to appeal to a guy who's anxious about making his charges "tougher." Per ASU players, Ziesel told them during the workout that he didn't drink water during combat and that "none of [the players] were worthy of his daughter."
articles.title: Will Matthew Mayich’s Collapse Change Anything?

At the start of Game 2 of their ALDS matchup Monday, Chicago White Sox starter-turned-reliever-turned-opener Anthony Kay faced the Cleveland Guardians offense and posed a powerful question. What would be more powerful: a papal blessing or Guardiansball, an offensive strategy best defined by the example phrase of "Steven Kwan infield single"? Well, immediately after the bottom of the first inning, Guardiansball was winning out.
Kwan himself led off affairs by hitting a ground ball that trickled its way out of the infield for a single. José Ramírez walked. Chase DeLauter moved both runners into scoring position with another ground ball. Kay was pulled for White Sox reliever-stayed-reliever Sean Newcomb, who immediately went down 2-0 in the count to Jo Adell, before intentionally walking him. Nathaniel Lowe came up to bat and then booped a high chop that bounced right to Newcomb. The Guardians then implemented the second core piece of their strategy, "opposing team forgets how to place defense." Newcomb whipped the ball way off mark for a throwing error, allowing two runs to score. He went on to strike out the next two batters. And so the fourth-worst slugging team in baseball this year ended the first inning with a two-run lead, despite failing to elevate the ball even once.
It was the first time in the White Sox's 2026 playoff run that the team started a game trailing and, permitting me to take even more indulgence in small playoff sample sizes, the first runs scored in by the Guardians in the series. The circumstances were in place for the White Sox's blessed playoff run to stall out, with the Guardians at home, their starter Gavin Williams well-rested and regularly hitting triple digits on the radar gun, and the White Sox's strategy of generously deploying openers looking suspiciously close to a cheap knock-off version of the Dodgers' "Oops, all starting pitchers!" approach to bullpen construction.

But in the three playoff games they’ve played so far, the latest a 92-82 home win over New York to open the second round, Karl Smesko's team has totally set the terms. As they see it, this is playoff basketball: fast, tireless, always connected. 
Even when the Dream bump into issues running their halfcourt offense, they make the math work for them in other ways. The best offensive rebounder in league history wins them extra possessions, and a team defense that’s forced more turnovers than any other WNBA team this year sets up easy scoring opportunities against defenses on their heels. That made them a nightmare first-round matchup for the Washington Mystics, who turned the ball over more than any other WNBA team this year. Washington’s season indeed ended thanks to a 42-15 turnover differential across two games.
Lest that stat be blamed on the young Mystics’ nerves, consider the 32 points Atlanta scored off 21 turnovers from veteran-stocked New York in Sunday's game. The fix for Game 2 on Wednesday sounds easy: Don’t turn the ball over. But the Atlanta Dream are a team designed to make it difficult. The Liberty’s problems weren’t all self-inflicted.
